sources: https://www.mdcalc.com/calc/1042/pittsburgh-knee-rules
https://radiopaedia.org/articles/pittsburgh-knee-rules?lang=us
Seaberg DC, Jackson R. Ann Emerg Med. 1994 — blunt trauma/fall + (age <12 or >50 or unable 4 steps); high sensitivity

issues: whyUse claimed 'high sensitivity for hip fracture' as if a validated Ottawa-style rule; PubMed has no Stiell hip radiography decision rule (cited PMID 9403421 is Ottawa Knee implementation), and next-step clinical cues remain reasonable without that claim.

changes.from: Supports selective imaging while retaining high sensitivity for hip fracture.
changes.to: Structures common high-yield cues for hip radiographs after trauma; occult fracture still possible if nonambulatory.

sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9403421/ (Stiell et al. JAMA 1997 — Ottawa Knee Rule implementation, not hip)
https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=Stiell+hip+radiography+decision (0 hits)
Standard ED practice: image post-fall hip/groin pain with inability to walk; MRI/CT if plain films negative and nonambulatory
https://www.mdcalc.com/calc/1817/kocher-criteria-septic-arthritis
Kocher MS et al. JBJS 1999 — non-weight-bearing, fever >38.5°C, ESR ≥40, WBC >12k; risk rises with criteria count
Caird MS et al. JBJS 2006 — CRP addition; urgent aspiration/OR for higher scores / toxic child
https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/injuries-poisoning/sprains-and-other-soft-tissue-injuries/achilles-tendon-tears
Thompson test ~96% sensitive / ~93% specific for complete Achilles rupture; plantaris/partial tears may be false-negative
Management: equinus brace / NWB pathway, urgent ortho, operative vs nonoperative discussion
Salter RB, Harris WR. JBJS 1963 — types I–V physeal injury classification
Types I–II generally closed reduction/immobilization; III–IV often need anatomic reduction ± fixation; V highest growth-arrest risk / often retrospective
https://www.orthobullets.com/trauma/1003/gustilo-classification
Gustilo RB, Anderson JT. JBJS 1976 — open fracture types I–IIIC
All open fractures: early IV antibiotics (type/contamination-guided), tetanus, dressing/splint, urgent I&D; IIIB plastics, IIIC vascular
https://radiopaedia.org/articles/mirels-classification-pathological-fracture-risk-1?lang=us
Mirels H. Clin Orthop Relat Res. 1989 — ≤7 low risk (~5%) radiotherapy/observation; 8 intermediate (~15%); ≥9 high (~33%+) prophylactic fixation
Functional/mechanical pain is a high-weight clinical factor in fixation counseling
https://www.orthobullets.com/trauma/1037/femoral-neck-fractures
Garden I–II nondisplaced (typically fixation); III–IV displaced (arthroplasty in elderly; fixation in selected young)
Young displaced: urgent reduction/fixation to limit osteonecrosis risk; hip-fracture time-to-OR pathways for elderly
Neer CS 2nd. JBJS 1970 — parts displaced if ≥1 cm or ≥45°
1-part: sling, early rehab; multi-part / head-split / fracture-dislocation: ortho, CT planning, document axillary nerve
https://radiopaedia.org/articles/weber-classification-of-ankle-fractures?lang=us
Danis-Weber A infrasyndesmotic (usually stable if isolated); B transsyndesmotic (stability variable); C suprasyndesmotic (usually unstable, syndesmosis risk)
Unstable B/C: NWB splint, ORIF ± syndesmotic fixation; examine proximal fibula for Maisonneuve
Leonard JC et al. Ann Emerg Med. 2011 (PMID 21035905) — risk factors associated with pediatric CSI after blunt trauma
This calculator is an educational risk-factor helper (not the later 2024 formal PECARN CSI prediction rule alone)
AMS/focal deficit: immobilize and image; no listed factors + normal cooperative exam may allow clinical clearance per protocol
https://reference.medscape.com/calculator/356/injury-severity-score
Baker SP et al. J Trauma. 1974 — ISS = sum of squares of three highest AIS region scores
Major trauma commonly ISS >15 (equivalently ≥16 for integer scores); registries/research severity metric after AIS coding
Osler T et al. J Trauma. 1997 (PMID 9420106) — three highest AIS injuries regardless of region
Often better mortality discrimination than ISS when multiple severe injuries share one body region
Boyd CR et al. J Trauma. 1987 — TRISS survival probability from RTS, ISS, age, blunt vs penetrating
Appropriate for audit/QI/education; ATLS priorities supersede score for bedside care
https://asia-spinalinjury.org/international-standards-neurological-classification-sci-isncsci-worksheet/
ASIA Impairment Scale A–E from ISNCSCI exam (traumatic and nontraumatic SCI)
Acute SCI: protect cord, perfusion MAP goals per protocol, urgent imaging/spine consult, DVT ppx, skin care
Frankel HL et al. Paraplegia 1969 — historical five-grade SCI scale preceding ASIA IS
Prefer modern ASIA IS + neurological level of injury for documentation; A–C need full SCI pathway
Jennett B, Bond M. Lancet 1975 — GOS 1 death through 5 good recovery
GOS 2–3: intensive rehab / goals of care; GOS 4–5: outpatient neuro follow-up and reintegration guidance

issues: nextSteps condition 'GOS-E ≤4' included death (GOS-E 1) in a rehab/caregiver action pathway; parallel GOS text correctly starts at grade 2.

changes.to: condition 'GOS-E 2–4' (vegetative through upper severe disability; excludes death)

sources: Wilson JT et al. J Neurotrauma. 1998 (PMID 9726257) — GOS-E 1 death, 2 vegetative, 3–4 severe disability, 5–6 moderate, 7–8 good recovery
TBI research often bins unfavorable as GOS-E 1–4, but bedside rehab next steps apply to living survivors (2–4)
Fagan TJ. N Engl J Med. 1975 (PMID 1143310) — nomogram relating pre-test probability, LR, post-test probability
Educational Bayes tool; high post-test → treat/confirm; low post-test → rule-out pathway with attention to prior and imperfect LR
Standard EBM teaching: LR+ = sens/(1−spec); LR− = (1−sens)/spec
LRs are more transportable across prevalence than PPV/NPV; apply with Fagan nomogram / pre-test probability
